pos: n. (Alypius of Thagaste, d. c. 430, Augustine's closest friend, baptized with him at Milan in 387 and afterward bishop of Thagaste)
etymology: Latin form of the Greek alypios, ‘free from grief.’ Known to the church almost entirely through Books VI and VIII of Augustine's Confessions.
biblical_def: Alypius was Augustine's younger townsman and pupil, and the Confessions tell his story as a case study in how habit masters a decent man. At Carthage he was enslaved to the circus races and was cured by a chance remark in one of Augustine's lectures. At Rome, dragged by friends to the gladiatorial show, he kept his eyes shut until a roar of the crowd opened them; he looked, drank in the savagery, and went home a lover of blood. Paul's warning describes the mechanism exactly: “evil communications corrupt good manners” (1Co 15:33). Yet the same man refused a bribe as a legal assessor when the powerful pressed him. In the garden at Milan he took up the book after Augustine had read it, found the next words, “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye” (Rom 14:1), applied them to himself, and followed his friend into the faith without delay. He was baptized with Augustine by Ambrose at Easter 387 and later served as bishop of Thagaste. His life commends the friendship of Proverbs: “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines friend as one who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem and respect which lead him to desire his company and seek to promote his happiness.
webster_full: FRIEND, n. One who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem, respect and affection.
2. One not hostile; one who is on the same side.
3. A favourer; one who is propitious; as, a friend to virtue.
scriptures: Rom 14:1
Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.
Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
corruption_summary: Alypius is remembered as a minor character in someone else's conversion, which misses the point the Confessions make with him: the eye is a door, and a good man can be taken through it in a single afternoon.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern readers treat Alypius's fall at the arena as quaint — a scrupulous young man upset by a violent spectacle. Augustine treats it as a demonstration of the doctrine of sin. Alypius trusted his own resolve (absent in mind, he boasted, he would overcome both them and the show), and the boast was the beginning of the defeat. Our entertainment culture runs on the same confidence: that a man can watch anything, because watching is not doing. The Scriptures never grant the premise; they guard the eye because the eye feeds the heart.

The corrective is not withdrawal from all company but the right company. Alypius was dragged down by friends and lifted up by a friend. The church has always needed both warnings: “evil communications corrupt good manners” (1Co 15:33), and, in the other direction, a brother who will read the next verse to you and take it as meant for himself. The recovery is ordinary Christian friendship — men who keep one another out of the arena and bring one another to the Word.
roots_summary: Greek homilia (G3657), companionship, communication; proslambano (G4355), to receive, take to oneself; Hebrew re'a (H7453), friend, companion.
roots_lines: Greek homilia (G3657) — company, communication; 1 Corinthians 15:33, the only New Testament use.
Greek proslambano (G4355) — to receive, take to oneself; Romans 14:1, 15:7.
Hebrew re'a (H7453) — friend, companion, neighbour; Proverbs 17:17, 27:17.
usage: “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye” (Rom 14:1) — the verse Alypius took for his own in the garden at Milan.
“evil communications corrupt good manners” (1Co 15:33) — the lesson of the arena at Rome.
“Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17) — the friendship that brought him to the font.

pos: n. (Nebridius, d. c. 390, Carthaginian friend of Augustine who left his home to seek the truth with him at Milan)
etymology: Latin personal name. He appears in Books IV, VI, VII and IX of the Confessions and in a surviving exchange of letters with Augustine.
biblical_def: Nebridius left a comfortable estate near Carthage and his mother's house to live at Milan with Augustine, for no other reason, the Confessions say, than to search with him for truth and wisdom. Job's question was his: “where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?” (Job 28:12). He was the sharper mind of the circle and supplied the argument that loosened Augustine from the Manichees: if the God of light could suffer harm from the kingdom of darkness, He was not incorruptible; and if He could not, there was no reason for the war the Manichees described. He came to faith after Augustine, was baptized, brought his whole household to Christ, and died young in Africa. Augustine closes his memory of him with confidence, not grief: his friend now lives in Abraham's bosom. The comfort is Paul's, that believers “sorrow not, even as others which have no hope” (1Th 4:13). The friendship itself fits the psalm: “We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company” (Psa 55:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines truth as conformity to fact or reality; the exact accordance of that which is asserted with that which exists.
webster_full: TRUTH, n. Conformity to fact or reality; exact accordance with that which is, or has been, or shall be.
2. True state of facts or things.
3. Veracity; purity from falsehood.
scriptures: But where shall wisdom be found? and where is the place of understanding?
A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company.
But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope.
corruption_summary: Nebridius is the friend who reasons, and his memory corrects the modern habit of treating argument as hostile to friendship and doubt as a permanent address.
corruption_paragraphs: The present age honours the seeker and distrusts the finder. To be “on a journey” is admired; to arrive is thought arrogant. Nebridius was a seeker of the old kind: he searched because he expected there was something to find, and when he found it he stopped searching and started obeying. His argument against the Manichees was not a debating trick but a clean piece of reasoning about the nature of God, and it did a friend real good.

The corrective is to recover the dignity of hard thinking among friends. Christian friendship is not only shared feeling; it is “sweet counsel” (Psa 55:14), which includes telling a friend his position does not hold. A friend who will not argue with you will not save you from error. Nebridius argued, and then he walked with his friends into the house of God.
roots_summary: Hebrew chokmah (H2451), wisdom; sod (H5475), counsel, intimate converse; Greek elpis (G1680), hope.
roots_lines: Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; Job 28:12, 28:28, Proverbs 4:7.
Hebrew sod (H5475) — counsel, intimate converse; Psalm 55:14, 25:14.
Greek elpis (G1680) — hope; 1 Thessalonians 4:13, 5:8.
usage: “where shall wisdom be found?” (Job 28:12) — the question that brought Nebridius to Milan.
“We took sweet counsel together” (Psa 55:14) — friendship that reasons together and worships together.
“that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope” (1Th 4:13) — how Augustine remembered him.

pos: n. (Simplicianus of Milan, d. 400/401, presbyter who instructed Ambrose and succeeded him as bishop of Milan)
etymology: Latin personal name from simplex, simple, single. Appears in Book VIII of the Confessions; Augustine's treatise To Simplicianus (396) answered his questions on Romans.
biblical_def: Simplicianus was the aged presbyter of Milan whom Ambrose himself had looked to as a father in the faith, and to him Augustine went when he could no longer bear his own divided will. Simplicianus did not argue; he told a story. He had known Marius Victorinus, the great rhetorician of Rome, and he told how that proud man had at last made his public profession before the congregation. The story did its work, and Augustine says he burned to imitate it. It is pastoral wisdom of a very old kind: “Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow” (Heb 13:7). Simplicianus was one of the faithful men of Paul's charge: “commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). Ten years later, now a bishop, Augustine sent him the answers to his questions on Romans 7 and 9 — the treatise in which Augustine first saw clearly that election is “not of works, but of him that calleth” (Rom 9:11). Simplicianus succeeded Ambrose as bishop of Milan in 397.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines counsel as advice; opinion or instruction given upon request or otherwise, for directing the judgment or conduct of another.
webster_full: COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction, given upon request or otherwise, for directing the judgment or conduct of another.
2. Consultation; interchange of opinions.
3. Prudence; deliberate opinion or judgment.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
For though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers: for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel.
Rom 9:11
(For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth;)
corruption_summary: Simplicianus is barely known, and that is the point the modern church misses: the most consequential ministry is often an old pastor telling a younger man what God has done for someone else.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern church looks for influence in platforms, and its counselling has drifted toward technique. Simplicianus had neither. He had a long memory, a store of true stories about grace, and the patience to let a troubled man hear one of them. Paul's distinction is exact: “though ye have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet have ye not many fathers” (1Co 4:15). The church is never short of instructors.

The recovery is the deliberate cultivation of spiritual fathers — older men who will receive the younger, hear them, and point them to Christ by the example of saints who went before. Simplicianus sat with Augustine once, and it changed the history of the Western church.
roots_summary: Greek paratithemi (G3908), to commit, entrust; mimeomai (G3401), to imitate, follow; pater (G3962), father.
roots_lines: Greek paratithemi (G3908) — to commit to one's charge; 2 Timothy 2:2, 1 Timothy 1:18.
Greek mimeomai (G3401) — to imitate, follow; Hebrews 13:7, 2 Thessalonians 3:7.
Greek pater (G3962) — father, used of a spiritual father; 1 Corinthians 4:15.
usage: “commit thou to faithful men” (2Ti 2:2) — the ministry Simplicianus received and passed on.
“yet have ye not many fathers” (1Co 4:15) — what Augustine found in the old presbyter.
“not of works, but of him that calleth” (Rom 9:11) — the truth Augustine worked out in answering his questions.

pos: n. (Gaius Marius Victorinus, 4th century, African-born rhetorician at Rome whose late public conversion is told in Book VIII of the Confessions)
etymology: Latin personal name from victor, conqueror. Translator into Latin of the Neoplatonic books Augustine read at Milan, and afterward a writer against the Arians.
biblical_def: Marius Victorinus was the most celebrated teacher of rhetoric in Rome, honoured with a statue in the Forum, and for most of his life a defender of the old gods. He translated the Platonist books into Latin and studied the Christian Scriptures with care. Privately he told Simplicianus that he was already a Christian. Simplicianus replied that he would not believe it until he saw him in the church, and Victorinus mocked: ‘Do walls then make Christians?’ But the Word pressed him: “whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:33). He came at last, gave in his name for baptism, and, when the presbyters offered to let a man of his rank profess the faith privately, he refused, and recited the creed from the raised place before the whole congregation, which shouted his name for joy. Paul's order held for the orator as for anyone: “with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom 10:10). When Julian the Apostate forbade Christians to teach rhetoric, Victorinus gave up his school.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines profession as the act of professing or claiming; open declaration; public avowal or acknowledgment of one's sentiments or belief.
webster_full: PROFESSION, n. The act of professing or claiming; open declaration; public avowal or acknowledgment of one's sentiments or belief.
2. The business which one professes to understand and to follow for subsistence; calling; vocation.
3. The act of entering into a religious order.
scriptures: Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.
But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven.
For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
Mar 8:38

Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation; of him also shall the Son of man be ashamed, when he cometh in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.
corruption_summary: Victorinus's question — ‘Do walls then make Christians?’ — is the creed of every private believer who will not join a church, and the Confessions answer it.
corruption_paragraphs: The private Christian is now a type: he believes, he reads, he may even pray, but he will not be numbered with a congregation, will not be baptized before witnesses, will not submit to elders. He asks Victorinus's question and thinks it unanswerable. The Scriptures answer it plainly. Confession of Christ is a mouth-and-heart act done “before men,” and the Lord attaches the promise to it, and the threat to its refusal.

Victorinus feared the mockery of his friends and the loss of standing; that is what kept him out of the church, and Augustine says so. The recovery is to treat public profession and church membership as obedience rather than ornament. A man of rank who stands up and recites the creed among plain believers has learned that the walls do not make Christians, but Christians do not stay outside them.
roots_summary: Greek homologeo (G3670), to confess, profess; arneomai (G720), to deny; epaischunomai (G1870), to be ashamed of.
roots_lines: Greek homologeo (G3670) — to confess, say the same thing; Matthew 10:32, Romans 10:9–10.
Greek arneomai (G720) — to deny, disown; Matthew 10:33, 2 Timothy 2:12.
Greek epaischunomai (G1870) — to be ashamed of; Mark 8:38, Romans 1:16.
usage: “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men” (Mat 10:32) — the word that brought the orator into the church.
“with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom 10:10) — why he would not profess in private.
“Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of me and of my words” (Mar 8:38) — the fear that kept him out so long.

pos: n. (Pontitianus, 4th century, African Christian at the imperial court whose visit in Book VIII of the Confessions preceded Augustine's conversion)
etymology: Latin personal name. Augustine names him as a fellow countryman from Africa who held high office in the emperor's service.
biblical_def: Pontitianus called on Augustine and Alypius at Milan on some business, noticed a book on the gaming table, and found it to be the epistles of Paul. He was a baptized Christian and was glad. He began to talk, and told them what they had never heard: the life of Antony of Egypt, who on hearing the Gospel read, “go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor” (Mat 19:21), had taken it as spoken to himself. Then he told of two court officials at Trier who, walking in a garden, found a copy of the life of Antony, read it, and resolved on the spot to leave the emperor's service for Christ's. As he spoke, Augustine says, God was turning him round to look at himself, and he could not bear what he saw. Within the hour he was in the garden where the conversion came. Pontitianus never knew what he had done. His part was the plain one Paul describes: “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14). A layman's conversation about what God had done for others was the instrument God used.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines testimony as a solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact; witness; evidence.
webster_full: TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration or affirmation made for the purpose of establishing or proving some fact.
2. Affirmation; declaration.
3. Witness; evidence; proof of some fact.
scriptures: Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me.
How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
So likewise, whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple.
Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee.
corruption_summary: Pontitianus is the forgotten evangelist of the Confessions, and his visit rebukes the idea that witness belongs to professionals or requires a programme.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern church has largely handed evangelism to specialists and to scripted methods. Pontitianus had no method. He had come on business, saw Paul's epistles lying on a table, and spoke of what he knew: the lives of believers who had taken Christ's words seriously. That is how the Gospel has always run from house to house — the testimony of the redeemed about the works of God, as the psalm promises: “Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee” (Psa 51:13).

His stories were about monks, and the Reformed reader should be clear that Christ's call to forsake all (Luk 14:33) is not a call to the cloister but to the cost of discipleship in every station. Yet the principle stands: a Christian who will speak of what grace has done, at the moment the door opens, may be the voice God uses to turn a man to look at himself.
roots_summary: Greek kerusso (G2784), to proclaim; apotassomai (G657), to forsake, bid farewell to; Hebrew shub (H7725), to turn, be converted.
roots_lines: Greek kerusso (G2784) — to herald, proclaim; Romans 10:14–15.
Greek apotassomai (G657) — to renounce, forsake; Luke 14:33.
Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn back, be converted; Psalm 51:13, 19:7.
usage: “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — a visitor at the gaming table was God's preacher that day.
“go and sell that thou hast” (Mat 19:21) — the text in the story Pontitianus told.
“sinners shall be converted unto thee” (Psa 51:13) — the fruit of one conversation.

pos: n. (Verecundus of Milan, d. c. 387, grammarian who lent Augustine his country house at Cassiciacum)
etymology: Latin personal name, “modest, bashful,” from vereor, to revere, fear. Remembered in Book IX of the Confessions.
biblical_def: Verecundus was a citizen and teacher of grammar at Milan, a close friend of Augustine's circle, and not yet a Christian when the others were converted. He grieved that he could not join them, for his wife was a believer and he thought marriage itself held him back from the full Christian life he imagined they had chosen. Yet he gave what he had. He lent them his country house at Cassiciacum for the months before their baptism, and there they prayed, read the Psalms, and wrote. Augustine prays that God will repay him with the freshness of the eternal paradise for the rest he gave them. The kindness is Scripture's: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2); “Use hospitality one to another without grudging” (1Pe 4:9). Christ's promise covers it: whoever gives “a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward” (Mat 10:42). Verecundus fell sick while Augustine was at Rome, believed, was baptized, and died in the faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hospitality as the act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.
webster_full: HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.
2. Hospitable treatment.
scriptures: Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.
Use hospitality one to another without grudging.
And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward.
corruption_summary: Verecundus believed marriage was a lesser road to God, an error of his age, and the Reformation answers it; his hospitality is the part of him worth recovering.
corruption_paragraphs: Verecundus's hesitation came from the ascetic temper of the fourth century, which ranked celibacy above marriage and made married believers feel like second-class Christians. The Reformers rejected that ranking. Marriage is honourable in all (Heb 13:4), a believing wife is a gift and not an obstacle, and a married layman serving God in his calling is not on a lower road than a monk.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What should be recovered is the ordinary grace of his open house. Christian hospitality does not require wealth; it requires a door and a willingness to share what is behind it. A borrowed villa became the place where Augustine prepared for baptism.
roots_summary: Greek philoxenia (G5381), hospitality, love of strangers; aphilarguros, without grudging (cf. gongusmos, G1112, murmuring); Hebrew ger (H1616), stranger, sojourner.
roots_lines: Greek philoxenia (G5381) — love of strangers, hospitality; Romans 12:13, Hebrews 13:2.
Greek gongusmos (G1112) — murmuring, grudging; 1 Peter 4:9.
Hebrew ger (H1616) — stranger, sojourner; Leviticus 19:34.
usage: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2) — the grace of the open house.
“Use hospitality one to another without grudging” (1Pe 4:9) — what Verecundus gave freely.
“he shall in no wise lose his reward” (Mat 10:42) — Christ's word over every cup of cold water.

pos: n. (Adeodatus, c. 372–c. 389, Augustine's son, baptized with him at Milan and dead in youth)
etymology: Latin a Deo datus, ‘given by God.’ Augustine's partner in the dialogue On the Teacher.
biblical_def: Adeodatus was born to Augustine and the woman he lived with for some fifteen years at Carthage, before he was married or converted. Augustine calls him the son of his sin, and yet he named him ‘given by God,’ and the name was truer than the father knew. The Confessions marvel at his gifts: by fifteen he outstripped many learned men, and the dialogue On the Teacher preserves his part in a conversation with his father about how words signify. He was baptized with Augustine and Alypius at Easter 387, of the same age in grace, as Augustine says. Within a few years he was dead. Augustine writes of him without anxiety. The psalm had taught him that “children are an heritage of the LORD” (Psa 127:3), and that “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (Jas 1:17) — even a gift given through a sinful union and taken back early. His confidence is David's at the death of his child: “I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me” (2Sa 12:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gift as a present; anything given or bestowed; that which is voluntarily transferred by one person to another without compensation.
webster_full: GIFT, n. A present; any thing given or bestowed; any thing, the property of which is voluntarily transferred by one person to another without compensation.
2. The act of giving or conferring.
3. Power; faculty; some quality or endowment conferred by the author of our nature.
scriptures: Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.
Jas 1:17
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
But now he is dead, wherefore should I fast? can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.
As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth.
corruption_summary: Adeodatus is the child of a sin, and his story contradicts two opposite errors — that such a child is a mistake, and that the sin which produced him was no sin.
corruption_paragraphs: One error treats a child born outside marriage as a misfortune and nothing more; the other, now dominant, treats the union itself as morally neutral and objects to calling it sin at all. Augustine refuses both. He calls the relationship what it was, confesses it, and in the same breath calls his son a gift of God. The Scriptures permit him both statements because the child's existence is from God even when the parents' conduct was not.

The recovery is that double honesty. The church must call fornication by its name, and it must receive every child as an heritage of the Lord, given a name and brought to the font and the Word. Adeodatus was both the son of his father's sin and a brother in grace, baptized beside his father on the same morning.
roots_summary: Hebrew nachalah (H5159), inheritance, heritage; Greek dosis (G1394), giving, and dorema (G1434), gift; Hebrew chatsir (H2682), grass.
roots_lines: Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — inheritance, heritage; Psalm 127:3.
Greek dosis (G1394) and dorema (G1434) — a giving, a gift; James 1:17.
Hebrew chatsir (H2682) — grass, the figure of brief human life; Psalm 103:15, Isaiah 40:6.
usage: “children are an heritage of the LORD” (Psa 127:3) — the truth inside the name Adeodatus.
“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (Jas 1:17) — a gift even through a sinful union.
“I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me” (2Sa 12:23) — a father's hope at a son's early death.

pos: n. (Evodius of Uzalis, d. 424, townsman of Augustine from Thagaste, present at Monica's death and afterward bishop of Uzalis)
etymology: Greek euodios, ‘of a good journey,’ cf. Euodias of Php 4:2. Appears in Book IX of the Confessions.
biblical_def: Evodius came from Thagaste, served as an agent in the imperial service, was converted and baptized before Augustine, and left the world's business to join the household of friends who were returning to Africa. He was with them at Ostia when Monica died. As the household broke into weeping, Evodius took up the psalter and began to sing Psalm 101, “I will sing of mercy and judgment” (Psa 101:1), and the whole house answered him. That is a friend's work: Scripture put into the mouths of the grieving when they cannot find words of their own. Solomon's sentence describes such a companion: “Two are better than one” (Ecc 4:9), for “if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow” (Ecc 4:10). In later life Evodius became bishop of Uzalis in Africa, corresponded with Augustine on hard questions of the soul, and appears as his partner in the dialogue On Free Choice of the Will. Like Timothy he was a man who would “naturally care” for the state of others (Php 2:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines companion as one who keeps company with another; one with whom a person frequently associates and converses; an associate; a comrade.
webster_full: COMPANION, n. One who keeps company with another; one with whom a person frequently associates and converses.
2. A partner; an associate.
3. A fellow; a mate.
scriptures: Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Ecc 4:10
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.
Php 2:20
For I have no man likeminded, who will naturally care for your state.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
corruption_summary: Evodius is remembered for a psalm sung at a deathbed, and that moment corrects the modern belief that grief must be managed by technique rather than met with the Word.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern funeral has largely abandoned the psalter for personal tributes, and the counselling of the bereaved has drifted toward a vocabulary of stages and processes. Evodius did something older and better. When the household was overwhelmed, he did not analyse their grief; he gave it a voice from Scripture, and a psalm of mercy and judgment steadied the whole house.

The recovery is to put the Psalms back into the mouths of the sorrowing — at the bedside, at the grave, in the home. A friend who can begin the psalm when no one else can speak is a gift to any household, and the church should train men to be that friend.
roots_summary: Hebrew chaber (H2270), companion, fellow; Greek isopsuchos (G2473), likeminded; episkopos (G1985), overseer.
roots_lines: Hebrew chaber (H2270) — associate, companion; Ecclesiastes 4:10 uses the related idea of a fellow who lifts up.
Greek isopsuchos (G2473) — of like soul, likeminded; Philippians 2:20, the only New Testament use.
Greek episkopos (G1985) — overseer, bishop; Acts 20:28, 1 Timothy 3:1–2.
usage: “I will sing of mercy and judgment” (Psa 101:1) — the psalm Evodius began when Monica died.
“the one will lift up his fellow” (Ecc 4:10) — a friend's work in the house of mourning.
“Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28) — his later charge at Uzalis.

pos: n. (Patricius of Thagaste, d. c. 371, Augustine's pagan father, won to Christ late in life by his wife Monica)
etymology: Latin, “patrician, noble.” Not to be confused with Patrick of Ireland, whose Latin name was the same. Described in Books II and IX of the Confessions.
biblical_def: Patricius was a town councillor of Thagaste of modest means, hot-tempered and unfaithful to his wife. Augustine records that Monica never quarrelled with him when he was angry and never reproached him for his infidelities; she waited, and her conduct preached to him. It is Peter's word fulfilled almost to the letter: wives may win unbelieving husbands, “that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives” (1Pe 3:1). Patricius was baptized shortly before his death, when Augustine was about seventeen. As a father he was ambitious for his son's career and strained his small means to send him to Carthage for study, but Augustine says he cared nothing whether his son was chaste, so long as he was eloquent. The Confessions set that neglect against the apostolic charge: fathers are to bring up their children “in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4). Paul's question hung over the household for years: “what knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt save thy husband?” (1Co 7:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines father as he who begets a child; and, in a larger sense, one who exercises paternal care over another; a guardian or protector.
webster_full: FATHER, n. He who begets a child.
2. One who exercises paternal care over another; a guardian or protector.
3. The appellation of the first person in the adorable Trinity.
scriptures: Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands; that, if any obey not the word, they also may without the word be won by the conversation of the wives;
While they behold your chaste conversation coupled with fear.
For what knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt save thy husband? or how knowest thou, O man, whether thou shalt save thy wife?
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
corruption_summary: Patricius is the father who wanted a successful son more than a godly one, and that preference is now the ordinary ambition of Christian parents.
corruption_paragraphs: Patricius did not oppose religion in his house; he simply did not think it mattered beside the career. Many Christian homes have the same order of loves: test scores, scholarships and placements are pursued with sacrifice and urgency, while the child's soul is entrusted to whatever the youth programme provides. The Confessions record what that order produced in Augustine — a brilliant young man and a slave to his lusts.

Monica's half of the story corrects a different error: the belief that an unbelieving or ungodly husband must be won by argument and pressure. Peter teaches the opposite, and Monica's patient, chaste conduct is the classic illustration. The recovery for fathers is to put the nurture of the Lord first; for wives in a hard marriage, to trust the conversation that preaches without words.
roots_summary: Greek anastrophe (G391), conversation, manner of life; kerdaino (G2770), to win, gain; paideia (G3809), nurture, discipline.
roots_lines: Greek anastrophe (G391) — behaviour, manner of life; 1 Peter 3:1–2.
Greek kerdaino (G2770) — to gain, win; 1 Peter 3:1, 1 Corinthians 9:19.
Greek paideia (G3809) — training, nurture, discipline; Ephesians 6:4, Hebrews 12:5.
usage: “won by the conversation of the wives” (1Pe 3:1) — how Monica won Patricius.
“in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4) — the charge Patricius neglected.
“whether thou shalt save thy husband” (1Co 7:16) — the long hope of a believing wife.

pos: n. (Faustus of Milevis, 4th century, Manichaean bishop whose meeting with Augustine at Carthage in 383 began Augustine's break with the sect)
etymology: Latin faustus, fortunate. Milevis was a town of Numidia. Augustine answered his attack on the Old Testament in the thirty-three books Against Faustus. Not to be confused with Faustus Socinus.
biblical_def: Faustus was the great man of the Manichees in Africa, and for nine years Augustine's doubts were met with the promise that Faustus would come and resolve them. When he came, Augustine found him charming, fluent and modest — and ignorant of the very sciences on which the Manichaean books made their confident claims about the heavens. He had read some Cicero and a little Seneca, and he spoke well. To his credit he admitted he could not answer, and Augustine liked him the more for it. But the spell broke: eloquence was not truth. Paul had drawn the line long before: “my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1Co 2:4), and he warned, “lest any man should beguile you with enticing words” (Col 2:4). Faustus was the kind of teacher men gather when “after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears” (2Ti 4:3). Later, as bishop, Augustine answered his rejection of the Old Testament line by line.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eloquence as oratory; the expression or utterance of strong emotion in a manner adapted to excite correspondent emotions in others.
webster_full: ELOQUENCE, n. Oratory; the act or the art of speaking well, or with fluency and elegance.
2. The power of speaking with fluency and elegance.
3. Elegant language, uttered with fluency and animation.
scriptures: And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect.
Col 2:4
And this I say, lest any man should beguile you with enticing words.
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
corruption_summary: Faustus is the celebrity teacher whose fluency stands in for truth, and every generation of the church has had to discover, as Augustine did, that the two are not the same.
corruption_paragraphs: The pattern is perennial: a movement promises answers, defers them to a famous speaker, and when the speaker arrives the audience is too charmed to notice that the questions are not answered. In our day the platform does the work the lecture hall did in Carthage. A preacher's ease, warmth and timing persuade crowds of claims he has never examined, and the Manichaean confidence about the stars has its successors in confident popular theology about everything from the end times to the soul.

The recovery is Augustine's discovery: judge the content, not the delivery. Paul renounced “wisdom of words” (1Co 1:17) precisely so that faith would rest on what was said, not on how well it was said. Faustus's honesty in admitting his ignorance is the one thing about him worth imitating, and it was the honesty, not the eloquence, that helped Augustine.
roots_summary: Greek peithos (G3981), persuasive, enticing; pithanologia (G4086), persuasive speech; knetho (G2833), to itch, tickle.
roots_lines: Greek peithos (G3981) — persuasive, enticing; 1 Corinthians 2:4.
Greek pithanologia (G4086) — persuasive speech, plausible argument; Colossians 2:4.
Greek knetho (G2833) — to itch, have the ears tickled; 2 Timothy 4:3.
usage: “not with enticing words of man's wisdom” (1Co 2:4) — what Faustus had and Paul refused.
“lest any man should beguile you with enticing words” (Col 2:4) — the warning Augustine learned at Carthage.
“having itching ears” (2Ti 4:3) — the audience that makes a Faustus.
